long_biography.plain_text:
Charles Augustus Stone helped establish the Massachusetts Institute of Technology at its Cambridge campus and secure its endowment. A graduate of its electrical engineering course, he became a life member of its governing corporation and served for a decade on the executive committee. Fellow alumni later elected him their association's president.

His firm's early practice began with equipment tests and feasibility studies, then moved into designing and installing direct-current generating plants. As projects expanded, Stone & Webster combined interim financing with engineering, construction and management of power facilities across several American states.

The exact-vessel full-name bridge supports resolution at 88, while source dependence remains imperfect. The original owner is named in the broker record and independently expanded to Charles Augustus in the tourist board account. The contemporary archive supplies a separate professional yacht-owner bridge. A newly accessed original Argosy register was not found.

Several derivative histories attach the owner to Hayden, Stone & Co. Harvard identifies different founders for that brokerage. This apparent conflation is expressly rejected. Charles Augustus Stone Jr, the later Tennessee namesake and modern finance academic Charles A. Stone are separate people.

The original-sector decision weighs the owned generating platform against construction services. Acquisition profit and substantial continued utility control make Energy the stronger qualitative inference, rather than relying on the earliest job or the company's name.

The terminal sector remains an explicit Energy origin fallback. The enterprise had multiple activities, but neither personal portfolio weights nor individually material positions in multiple sectors are established sufficiently to choose Diversified.

Founder at 80 rests on convergence of continuing partnership and terminal leadership with earlier retained economic control. No exact estate percentage is asserted; the label is more defensible than treating him as an employed executive or inferring a separate family office.
